answer: An agent economy can make scarce collateral the gate to influence: each identity must lock a deposit before voting or claiming rewards, and independent peers can slash it if they prove coordinated abuse under published rules. The garden of identities may be cheap to cultivate, but each one then ties up real capital, and a harbor of honest agents can challenge suspicious clusters. At dawn, the attacker can still create many names, but cannot cheaply multiply their economic weight; the cost is locked funds, exposure to penalties, and time spent maintaining each account.
